When Mehak first said, "What if we just got one flat instead of two?", I said, "Yes, obviously," and meant it. Then over the next month I got quieter and quieter.
I love her. I love waking up to her humming and the way she argues with the TV news. But every time she sent me a listing, something in my chest tightened, like a door slowly swinging shut. No more evenings alone with my music loud. No more coming home to just me.
I didn't say anything, which I now know was the problem. Mehak thought I was losing interest. One night she asked, "Do you not want this?" and I finally said it: "I do. And I'm scared. Both."
She laughed, a bit shakily. "Thank god. I thought it was only the second one." After that, Disha's fear became something we could plan around, instead of something Mehak had to guess.

qa.q: What did Mehak first suggest?
qa.a: Mehak suggested getting one flat instead of two.

qa.q: Why did Disha go quiet over that month?
qa.a: Disha loved Mehak but felt a door closing on time alone and freedom, and didn't know how to say both feelings at once.

qa.q: What changed once Disha said 'I do. And I'm scared. Both.'?
qa.a: The mixed feelings became something they could plan around together, instead of Mehak guessing that Disha was losing interest.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling while Disha stayed quiet?
qa.a: Mehak thought Disha was losing interest and was worried, which is why her laugh was shaky with relief once Disha explained.

grounding: Shows one partner growing quiet as moving in together nears, feeling love and a closing door, and saying it before the silence does harm.

Chandrika came alone today. She has been with her partner, Dev, for two years, and in recent weeks he has begun talking about moving in together.

She described becoming quieter each time the subject comes up. "I love him. I really do. But when he showed me flats on his phone, I felt like a door was closing." She spoke fast, then stopped, looking embarrassed.

She said she has not told Dev any of this, because she fears he will hear it as rejection. Meanwhile she has started working late and avoiding weekend plans. She recognised this herself: "I'm hiding in the office."

I told her that mixed feelings about a big step are common and that the greater risk is hiding them. We discussed how she might tell Dev early, in her own words, that she loves him and also feels scared. She agreed to try this week.

— Sarika

Sunday night

Gautam brought up moving in again at dinner. He's so excited. He's already chosen which room would be the study.

And I just... went quiet. Again. Third time this month.

I love him. That part isn't the question. But when I picture it, my own flat gone, my Sunday mornings alone with the newspaper and nobody to talk to, something in my chest tightens. Like a door I can't open again.

I told myself I'd sort it out in my head first. But it's been weeks and I'm hiding it by being "tired" every time he brings it up. That's not fair to him.

Tomorrow I'm going to say it: "I want this, and I'm scared of it. Both." Better he hears it now than after we've signed a lease.

— Minakshi

qa.q: What has Gautam already chosen for the new home?
qa.a: Which room would be the study.

qa.q: What does the tightening in Minakshi's chest reveal?
qa.a: It reveals fear of losing her freedom and her own space, even though she loves Gautam.

qa.q: Why is Minakshi's plan for tomorrow a kind choice?
qa.a: Saying early that she wants this and is scared of it lets Gautam understand, instead of being confused by her being "tired".

qa.q: How might Gautam feel when Minakshi tells him?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and a little hurt at first, but also relieved to understand why she has gone quiet.

In the tailoring shop by Sirsa's bus stand, Sarita pinned a blouse and missed the pin twice. Nikita, stitching at the next machine, noticed. For a week Sarita had been quiet, ever since Hemant's mother began talking about which room would be theirs after the wedding in March.
"You love him, na?" Nikita asked.
"I do. That's the trouble," Sarita said. "I love him, and I also keep thinking of this shop, my late evenings, my own key. It feels like a door shutting slowly."
That evening, when Hemant rang, she almost said, "All fine." Instead she said, "Can I tell you something that scares me, before March and not after?"
There was a pause on the line. Then Hemant said, "Tell me. I'd rather know now."

qa.q: What had Hemant's mother begun talking about?
qa.a: She had begun talking about which room would be theirs after the wedding in March.

qa.q: How can you tell Sarita feels torn about the move?
qa.a: She misses the pin twice and has been quiet for a week; she says she loves Hemant yet fears losing her shop, her late evenings and her own key, so she feels torn and scared.

qa.q: What turning point does Sarita choose, and why is it kinder?
qa.a: She tells Hemant her fear before March instead of saying "All fine", so they can face it together rather than discover it after the wedding.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita, stitching beside Sarita this week?
qa.a: Nikita sees Sarita's silence and clumsy pinning and seems concerned enough to ask gently, giving her a safe first place to say what she feels.

grounding: Shows a young woman growing quiet as living together nears, feeling both love and a closing door, and choosing to say it early.
